## Findings by module

### 1

- **refined** (ch-065 chunk 1 (Keita, genetic connections)): Keita (2021, vol. IX): Africa's peoples are diverse and have long exchanged genes and languages (Bantu and Batwa gene flow circa 4000-1000 BCE, the Swahili as a first-millennium mixture, Taveta, Madagascar's Austronesian-speaking mix, Arabized Africans in the north, Songhai and Moroccan soldiers who stayed, Almoravids of diverse African peoples); the Sahara has 'always been traversable' and the north/sub-Saharan split is not a biological boundary; no living population is a 'race' in the biological sense and the word should be rejected 'on scientific and ethical grounds'; modern humans emerged in Africa at least 150,000-200,000 years ago (possible 300,000), left about 60,000-70,000 years ago. Uses Pagani 2015 for modern Egyptians as an amalgam of ancient local Nilotic-Saharan people with later arrivals. Module 1 ('Genetics is a sixth line'): use this as the concept: genetics shows connection and mixture, not racial blocks.
- **refined** (ch-086 chunk 2 (Bocoum, long-term argument)): Bocoum's wider claim: the iron bar import and the Atlantic slave trade pushed Africa into 'technological dependence' because Europe and China adopted indirect reduction (blast furnaces) and Africa used direct reduction at scale only in modern times; Luba smiths deliberately made steel (de Maret); Samori Toure grasped the dependence too late; he concludes that none of the Meroe, Carthage or North African routes can have supplied sub-Saharan iron because the sub-Saharan dates are older (his reading), the Termit/Niger and Oboui sites being most coherent, with 'the question still open'. The 'origins of under-development' argument is his thesis, not a result [CONTESTED]; include in Module 8 only as a named position beside Rodney. Module 1/5: the iron-bar claim has no date or tonnage in this chapter.
- **contradicted** (ch-086 chunk 1 (Bocoum, iron dating)): Bocoum (vol. IX) argues African iron smelting is independent and begins 'at least' in the second millennium BCE: Oboui (Central African Republic) furnaces and pits with 14C dates (2 sigma) around 2343-1900 BCE and Termit/Do Dimmi (Niger) dates from about 1666-1450 BCE, Table 1 lists many first-millennium BCE sites (Nsukka/Lejja, Mandara, Gabon, Togo, Burkina Faso); he calls Meroe and Carthage 'technically and chronologically disqualified' as sources, and Holl (1985) is cited that no furnace has been found in Carthaginian sites. He concedes Grebenart's Afunfun 'Copper I' furnace dates (1710 BCE; recalibrated 2450-1750 BCE) rested on mis-identified burnt tree stumps, and that Killick's fossil-charcoal objection (old-wood effect) applies to that case, but argues the Oboui series answers it (Salieges). He treats Killick and others as ideologically obstinate. The disagreement is live: the dates from Oboui (2400-800 BCE) are disputed in the literature he cites (Clist 2012 on disturbed stratigraphy, Killick 2015). Module 1 and 5: write 'iron-smelting in Africa began independently; the oldest claimed dates (about 2000 BCE in Central Africa, Niger) are disputed, and the secure minimum is by about 800-500 BCE' [CONTESTED].
- **extended** (ch-065 chunk 2 (Keita, Y haplogroups)): Keita's Y-chromosome case: haplogroup E (M96, about 50,000 years old, probably eastern tropical Africa) is the commonest Y lineage in all four African quadrants, so Africa's regions are 'connected via its men', and E1b1 lineages (including M35/E1b1b across the Horn, Egypt and the Maghrib) share deep ancestors in tropical Africa, so the Sahara is not a boundary; R1 reached the central Sahara perhaps 20,000 years ago from south-west Asia and was assimilated; J (north-east, Red Sea) and O (Madagascar) record contact with Asia; Ramses III's Y lineage read as E1b1a (Hawass et al. 2012) with a 'narrow set of markers' for the autosomal reading (Martin 2013, a commercial site) is the author's inference and is not drawn as a firm result. This is a single author's synthesis (Y lineages only, male-line, not whole genomes) and says 'Y evidence suggests', so the course should state: Y-chromosome E dominates Africa and links regions; it does not by itself prove skin colour or the ancient Egyptians' ancestry [CONTESTED].

### 2

- **refined** (ch-081 chunk 2 (Gourdine, conclusion)): Gourdine concedes that 'the ancient DNA data from predynastic and dynastic populations currently available are not representative of the entire history of Egypt' (few samples), calls them fragments of a puzzle and asks whether Pharaonic Egypt was 'a genetic mosaic' of Sahara, Lake Chad and Near East peoples; recommends more sequencing, autosomal markers and parasite DNA. The chapter's own list shows the field: Zink 2003 tuberculosis (M. africanum in early mummies), Marin 1999 sickle-cell markers (3 mummies), Khairat 2013 Greco-Roman mummies (mtDNA haplotype from Asia), Drosou 2018 two 12th-dynasty mummies (mtDNA M1a1, maybe siblings). Course line: the evidence is partial, mosaic, and contested; two readings (Gourdine/Hawass vs Schuenemann) differ because they used different sites, periods and markers [CONTESTED].
- **contradicted** (ch-081 chunk 1 (Gourdine, ancient DNA of Egypt)): Gourdine (vol. IX, 2021) sets out ancient-DNA work on Egypt and argues for an African contribution from the start: Adaima (Crubezy) modern inhabitants 74% Y-E1b1; the Hawass et al. 2010 and 2012 royal-mummy study (8 CODIS STR markers plus Y) found E1b1a in Ramses III; Gourdine's own use of the Pop Affiliator tool on the Amarna mummies gives 41-93.9% sub-Saharan affinity and he adds DNA Tribes company analysis (Martin 2012-13, commercial, not peer-reviewed) pointing to Great Lakes/Central/Southern affinities; he acknowledges those use only 8 of 13 markers. He sets against it Schuenemann et al. 2017 (Abusir el-Meleq, 151 mummies, 3 genomes), which concluded ancient Egyptians shared more Near Eastern ancestry than modern Egyptians who gained sub-Saharan ancestry later, and rebuts it as unrepresentative (3 genomes, one site, two periods, mtDNA mostly) [CONTESTED]. Two positions, a methods-limited debate; the course must name both and say that the Abusir result (peer-reviewed whole genomes) and the Amarna reading (STR tools, commercial site) use different data and neither covers all of Egypt or all of 3,000 years.

Totals: 0 confirmed, 3 refined, 2 contradicted, 1 extended, 0 absent, 0 note.
